title: The cell cycle and mitosis; Control of the cell cycle and cancer
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CD01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; CD01b#t3 term and clue written for the game; CD01b#t1 term and clue written for the game; CD01b#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD01b#N.2, CD02a#N.3, CD01b#N.5, CD02a#N.8, CD02a#N.10, CD02a#N.13a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anaphase
items.clue: Two groups of V-shaped chromatids are moving apart

items.label: Metaphase
items.clue: Chromosomes lie in a single line across the equator

items.label: Interphase
items.clue: Intact nucleus with no separate chromosomes visible; the look of most cells

items.label: Prophase
items.clue: Thread-like chromosomes lie scattered while the nuclear envelope disappears

questions.stem: Two cells are seen in a stained micrograph of a root tip. Cell 1 has an intact nucleus in which no separate chromosomes can be distinguished. Cell 2 has no nuclear envelope, and its condensed chromosomes lie in a single line across the middle of the cell. Which identification is correct?

options.text: Cell 1 is in prophase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in prophase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in early anaphase.

questions.explanation: An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes is a cell between divisions. Condensed chromosomes aligned at the equator, envelope gone, is metaphase.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of checkpoints in the cell cycle?

options.text: They are points at which a cell moves on automatically once it has grown to a certain size.
They are points at which the cell's progress is held until conditions for the next stage are met.
They are points at which any cell with a problem is destroyed at once, instead of being held there.
They are points in mitosis at which the cell's DNA is replicated, so each daughter cell gets a copy.

questions.explanation: At each checkpoint, conditions such as DNA damage, complete replication or spindle attachment are checked, and the cycle is halted until they are met.

questions.stem: In a stained root-tip squash, one cell shows two groups of V-shaped chromatids, their points facing opposite ends of the cell. Which explains this appearance?

options.text: The chromatids are repelling each other and drifting apart; the V shape is the drag of the cytoplasm.
Homologous chromosomes are being separated, each bent at the middle where it was paired.
It is anaphase: spindle fibres attached at each centromere pull it towards a pole, so the arms trail behind.
It is anaphase: the spindle fibres contract like muscle fibres, folding each chromatid in half.

questions.stem: The risk of developing most cancers rises steeply with age. Which explanation fits how tumours form?

options.text: Cells in older people divide faster because the body needs more replacement cells.
A single mutation present from birth suddenly switches on in later life and starts a tumour.
Cancer is simply fast division, and all body cells divide faster as the body ages.
Tumours usually need several mutations in one cell line, which take years to build up.

questions.explanation: Each control gene lost removes one restraint. Collecting several such mutations in one line of cells takes many divisions, and so usually many years.

questions.stem: A cell's DNA is severely damaged, and the damage cannot be repaired. The proteins that control the cell's checkpoints function normally. Which prediction about this cell is best supported?

options.text: It becomes a cancer cell, as any damage to a cell's DNA leads to the development of cancer.
It may still divide on schedule, as cells divide once they have grown large enough.
It is halted at a checkpoint and may undergo apoptosis, so the damage is not passed on.
It divides sooner than usual, as a damaged cell needs to be replaced by new ones.

questions.explanation: Checkpoint proteins halt the cell; if the damage cannot be repaired, it may undergo apoptosis. Either way it does not pass the damaged DNA to daughter cells.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical mammal, protein Q halts the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint when a cell's DNA is damaged and triggers apoptosis if the damage cannot be repaired. A mutation in a skin cell inactivates protein Q. Which statement best explains how this mutation can lead to cancer?

options.text: The cell then divides faster at every stage, and fast division is what makes a cell cancerous.
This single mutation is enough, on its own, to turn the cell into a cancer cell.
The damaged cell divides more often because it needs to replace the cells that died.
Cells with damaged DNA keep dividing, and further mutations build up in their descendants.
